Capacitors and Treble Bleeds Explained

Capacitors perform two different jobs depending on where they are used. In a tone circuit they form a frequency-dependent path to ground. Across a volume control they can form part of a treble bleed circuit.

In this article
Tone capacitors →Capacitor construction →What is a treble bleed? →Capacitor-only arrangements →Capacitor and resistor in parallel →Which should I choose? →

Tone capacitors

A capacitor’s opposition to alternating current decreases as frequency rises. In a guitar tone branch, the capacitor and tone potentiometer allow higher-frequency signal to reach ground more readily than lower-frequency signal. This is a branch off the signal path, not a component every part of the output must pass through.

As the tone control is rolled down, increasing capacitance generally extends the effect further into lower frequencies. The pickup’s inductance, pot resistance and other loads mean the result is more involved than a single fixed cutoff frequency.

These are starting points, not a quality ranking. Compare values with your actual pickups and how far you use the tone control. A value useful on one guitar may be excessive or too subtle on another.

Capacitor construction

Polyester film, polypropylene film and ceramic capacitors use different dielectric materials and constructions. Their specifications can differ in tolerance, stability, temperature behaviour and physical size. A voltage rating describes an operating limit, not an extra amount of “tone”.

Apparition focuses on correct capacitance, appropriate tolerance, measured value, reliable construction and a part that fits the cavity. Brand or price alone is not evidence of an audible benefit. Compare the actual specifications before assuming two capacitors with the same printed value behave differently in your guitar.

What is a treble bleed?

Rolling down a passive guitar’s volume can change the interaction between the pickup, volume pot and cable capacitance, often reducing high-frequency content. A treble bleed provides a frequency-dependent bypass between the volume control’s input and output.

Both Fender and Seymour Duncan describe circuits intended to retain more high-frequency content as volume is reduced. It is an optional response change, not a repair every guitar needs.

Capacitor-only arrangements

The simplest arrangement places a capacitor between volume input and wiper. Apparition’s examples are the 180pF PRS-style Treble Bleed and the 1nF Capacitor-only Treble Bleed. 1nF equals 0.001µF or 1,000pF.

The larger value passes more lower-frequency content through the bypass at a given impedance, but that does not make it better. The effect depends on the pot setting and surrounding circuit. At full volume the input and wiper are already very close electrically, so the bypass has little voltage across it.

View the 180pF example →

Capacitor and resistor in parallel

The 1nF + 150kΩ Duncan-style Treble Bleed connects a capacitor and resistor across the same two volume terminals. Parallel means both component ends share the corresponding input and output connections. The resistor provides a non-frequency-selective path alongside the capacitor and changes the volume control’s effective response and taper.

Do not confuse this with a capacitor and resistor in series. Their electrical behaviour is different. In a two-volume Apparition kit, the chosen bleed configuration is fitted to both volume controls.

View the parallel network →

Which should I choose?

Consider your pickup, pot value, cable capacitance, wiring circuit, volume-control habits and personal preference. If you like the way your guitar loses high end as you reduce volume, you may prefer no treble bleed. If you rely on a clearer reduced-volume sound, a bleed is worth comparing.

Our generator offers standard treble bleeds with Modern and 60s Les Paul wiring. It disables them for its 50s preset, where the tone branch already follows the volume output. This is the supported Apparition configuration, not a claim that every other circuit combination is physically impossible.

Values and units

1 µF = 1,000 nF = 1,000,000 pF. Common guitar tone values include 0.010, 0.015, 0.022, 0.033 and 0.047 µF, equivalent to 10, 15, 22, 33 and 47 nF. Compare supported values with the tone control position held constant. Tolerance changes the actual capacitance. The voltage rating is a permissible working limit, not a promise of a different guitar response. A large high-voltage part and a small part can have the same capacitance; dielectric, leakage, reliability and physical fit are specifications to consider without assuming an audible benefit from size or brand.
